betterCitation: Antonio Gramsci, Letters from Prison, letter to Carlo, Turi, 19 December 1929 (trans. Lynne Lawner, 1973)
reason: REFUTED on two counts, one of them decisive. FIRST, the provenance the card hides. I read the letter itself in Lynne Lawner's published translation (Letters from Prison, Quartet 1979, copyright 1973 Lynne Lawner, letter 41, headed Turi, December 19, 1929). Lawner hangs footnote 2 on this very sentence and the footnote says plainly that Romain Rolland “is the author of this famous phrase, which was quoted many times by Gramsci”, citing Gramsci's use of it in Ordine Nuovo on 30 April 1920. Frank Rosengarten, the editor of the very Columbia edition the verifier names, is the scholar who in 1994 located Rolland's own use of the formula in L'Humanité on 19 March 1920, weeks before Gramsci first reached for it. So the apparatus of BOTH English editions footnotes this line to Rolland, and the card would print it as Gramsci's own maxim under his byline with an empty provenance. The brief's misattribution appendix closes with exactly this duty, that a line one figure takes from another is the other's and the note says so, and this note says nothing about Rolland at all. It is not fatal that Gramsci is applying a borrowed motto to himself in the first person, but it is fatal that the note is silent about it while claiming, in capitals, to have been CORRECTED. SECOND, the wording claim is not closed. The verifier's whole case for Rosenthal is a single footnote in one magazine article, and that footnote actually names the Columbia printing of 2011, not the 1994 edition the source line credits; the source line therefore asserts a translation year the evidence does not carry. I could not reach Rosenthal's p. 299 to compare. What I CAN certify is the wording of the other translation, because I read it: Lawner renders the passage “My own state of mind synthesizes these two feelings and transcends them: my mind is pessimistic, but my will is optimistic.” That is not the card's English, so the verifier was right to drop Lawner, and wrong to think dropping her settled the question. The Italian is sound, confirmed on Italian sources as “Sono pessimista con l'intelligenza, ma ottimista per la volontà” in the letter of 19 dicembre 1929. Everything else passes: shipped.js reports not shipped, no near match, Gramsci unused and unbanned, and the source line is 112 characters with no dash. THE FIX, if the editor wants this line in July: ship Lawner's verified wording under the betterCitation source line above, and write a note that says the formula is Romain Rolland's, that Gramsci credited it to Rolland in Ordine Nuovo in April 1920, and that here he is turning it on himself in prison. Otherwise hold the line until someone opens Rosenthal's volume 1 at p. 299.
